questions.title: Neurilemmal sheath is important for nerve regeneration
questions.question: It is correct to say that:

options.A: dendrites conduct impulses away from the soma
options.B: axon conducts impulse toward the soma
options.C: neurilemmal sheath is important for nerve regeneration
options.D: neurilemmal sheath is a lipoprotein in nature
options.E: myelin is formed of single layer of Schwann cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dendrites conduct impulses toward the soma, not away from it -- the axon is the process that carries the impulse away from the cell body toward the next cell or target.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the axon's actual direction of conduction: the axon carries the impulse away from the soma, toward the terminal, not toward it.
explanations.C: Correct. The neurilemmal sheath (sheath of Schwann), the Schwann cell's own cytoplasm and nucleus forming the outermost covering of a peripheral axon, is what makes peripheral nerve regeneration possible after injury. It provides a physical guide -- a tube the Schwann cells maintain -- for a regrowing axon to follow back toward its original target. Central nervous system axons, which lack this neurilemmal sheath, do not have the same regenerative capacity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the myelin sheath, not the neurilemmal sheath, that is lipoprotein in composition -- the neurilemmal sheath is Schwann cell cytoplasm and nucleus, not a lipoprotein membrane structure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Myelin is formed of many concentric layers of compacted Schwann-cell membrane wrapped around the axon, not a single layer -- it is this multilayered wrapping that gives myelin its insulating property.

questions.learning_objective: State that the neurilemmal sheath is important for peripheral nerve regeneration, the same fact tested from the opposite direction in Q19 (the neurilemma's outermost-layer position).

field_notes.crossQuestionNote: Same concept as Q19 (already authored, cbf-bank-new cluster) -- Q19 asks where the neurilemma sits, this asks what it does; not a duplicate, per the pattern the concept's own field_notes already flags.

questions.title: Most important ion for resting membrane potential
questions.question: The most important ion during resting membrane potential is:

options.A: Na+
options.B: K+
options.C: Ca++
options.D: Cl–

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sodium's resting permeability is low compared with potassium's, so Na+ contributes only a small part of the resting potential -- it is the depolarizing ion once voltage-gated channels open, not the ion that sets the resting value.
explanations.B: Correct. The resting nerve membrane is far more permeable to potassium than to any other ion, through leak channels, which is why the resting membrane potential sits close to the potassium equilibrium potential. This K+ dominance, not the concentration gradients of the other ions alone, is what makes potassium the single most important ion in establishing the resting potential. Sodium, calcium and chloride each play smaller or later roles, but none dominates the resting state the way K+ does.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The resting membrane's permeability to calcium is very low; calcium instead plays a threshold-stabilising role at the channel level, not a leading role in setting the resting potential itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chloride crosses the resting membrane far less readily than potassium does in most excitable cells, so it does not dominate the resting potential the way K+ does.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bicarbonate is not a significant determinant of the resting membrane potential in nerve fibres; its role is chiefly in acid-base buffering, not membrane electrophysiology.

questions.learning_objective: Identify potassium as the ion whose resting permeability dominates and sets the resting membrane potential.

questions.title: RMP is mainly due to K+ efflux through leak channels
questions.question: Concerning the RMP:

options.A: it is mainly due to K+ influx through leak channels
options.B: it is mainly due to Na+ efflux
options.C: it is usually of fixed value in all tissues
options.D: it is mainly due to K+ efflux through leak channels
options.E: it is more negative in nerve fibers than muscle fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. This has the right ion but the wrong direction: potassium's concentration gradient favours efflux (outward movement) at rest, not influx, since intracellular K+ is far higher than extracellular K+.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sodium's resting permeability is low, so Na+ efflux is not the dominant driver of the resting potential; and physiologically Na+'s gradient favours influx at rest, not efflux.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The RMP is not fixed across all tissues -- it varies by cell type, larger (more negative) in large nerve and skeletal muscle fibres and smaller in less excitable cells such as red blood cells and epithelium.
explanations.D: Correct. The resting membrane is far more permeable to potassium than to any other ion, through leak channels, so K+ efflux down its concentration gradient is the main driver of the resting membrane potential. This is why the resting potential sits close to, though not exactly at, the potassium equilibrium potential. The small remaining gap is filled mainly by the electrogenic Na+-K+ pump.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This comparison is not the defining feature of the RMP mechanism, and RMP magnitude is generally described as similar in large nerve and large skeletal muscle fibres rather than one being characteristically more negative than the other.

questions.learning_objective: State that the resting membrane potential is mainly due to K+ efflux through leak channels.

questions.title: Depolarization brought about by increased sodium permeability
questions.question: During an action potential, depolarization of nerve cell membrane is brought about by:

options.A: increased sodium permeability
options.B: increased calcium permeability
options.C: increased chloride permeability
options.D: increased potassium permeability
options.E: both a and b are correct

explanations.A: Correct. Depolarization is caused by a rise in sodium permeability: voltage-gated Na+ channels open, Na+ moves down its steep electrochemical gradient into the cell, and this influx drives the membrane potential toward the sodium equilibrium potential. This is the rising phase of the action potential, and the size of the depolarization tracks the size of this permeability rise.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased calcium permeability is not the mechanism that produces the nerve action potential's depolarization phase (unlike in some cardiac and smooth muscle cells); calcium's role here is instead to stabilise Na+ channels at the resting membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increased chloride permeability moves the membrane potential toward the (negative) chloride equilibrium potential, stabilising or hyperpolarizing the membrane rather than depolarizing it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased potassium permeability drives the membrane potential toward the (negative) potassium equilibrium potential, producing repolarization or hyperpolarization, the opposite of depolarization.
explanations.E: Incorrect as a whole, since option B (calcium permeability) is not correct for the nerve action potential's depolarization -- only sodium permeability drives it.

questions.learning_objective: State that depolarization is caused by increased sodium permeability, distinguishing it from calcium's separate channel-stabilising role.

questions.title: Depolarization coincides with inability to respond to a further stimulus
questions.question: Depolarization in the nerve:

options.A: is caused by Na+ outflow
options.B: is caused by K+ outflow
options.C: is due to opening of inactivation gates of voltage gated Na+ channels
options.D: is represented by descending limb of the spike
options.E: is that during which the nerve can not respond to any stimulus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Depolarization is caused by Na+ inflow (influx down its electrochemical gradient), not outflow -- reversing the direction of Na+ movement here reverses the actual mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. K+ outflow drives repolarization, the return toward the resting level, not depolarization -- the two phases are driven by opposite ionic movements.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inactivation gates close, not open, as depolarization proceeds -- an open inactivation gate describes the resting, not the depolarizing, state of the channel.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Depolarization is represented by the ascending limb of the spike, not the descending limb -- the descending limb is repolarization.
explanations.E: Correct. Depolarization occupies roughly the same window as the absolute refractory period: once enough voltage-gated Na+ channels have opened and then had their inactivation gates close, no further stimulus, however strong, can trigger a second action potential until those channels recover. So depolarization is exactly the interval during which the nerve cannot respond to any stimulus. Only once repolarization is well underway and enough channels have recovered does the fibre regain the ability to fire again.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that depolarization coincides with the absolute refractory period, during which no stimulus of any strength can excite the fibre.

questions.title: Excitability decreases markedly during depolarization
questions.question: During depolarization of nerve fiber:

options.A: sodium ions move to the outside due to activation of voltage gated sodium channels
options.B: excitability decreases markedly
options.C: potassium ions move to the outside due to activation of voltage gated potassium channels
options.D: the membrane potential changes from – 90 mv to maximally – 10 mv

explanations.A: Incorrect. Activation of voltage-gated sodium channels lets Na+ move into the cell, not to the outside -- this option has the right channel but the wrong direction of ion movement.
explanations.B: Correct. As depolarization proceeds, voltage-gated Na+ channels' separate inactivation gates begin closing on a short delay, and once enough of them are closed the fibre enters the absolute refractory period. Excitability therefore falls sharply during depolarization, from its initial rise near the firing level to essentially zero as the channels needed for a second action potential become unavailable.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is voltage-gated sodium, not potassium, channels that activate during depolarization; potassium channel activation (and the resulting K+ efflux) is the mechanism of repolarization, which follows depolarization.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Depolarization overshoots the resting level and reverses the membrane potential to a positive value (around +35 mV in the standard teaching figures), not merely to a less negative value such as -10 mV.
explanations.E: Incorrect, since option D is not correct and option C misassigns potassium channel activation to the depolarization phase rather than to repolarization.

questions.learning_objective: State that excitability decreases markedly during depolarization, as Na+ channel inactivation gates close and the fibre approaches the absolute refractory period.

field_notes.authorDoubt: The printed key (b) tests the onset of the absolute refractory period during depolarization, which is physiologically consistent (no second, disagreeing mark exists for this item) -- not held.

questions.title: Ascending limb of the spike represents depolarization
questions.question: The ascending limb of the spike potential in the nerve:

options.A: is caused by K+ inflow
options.B: represents depolarization
options.C: is caused by Na+ inflow through leak channels
options.D: represents Repolarization

explanations.A: Incorrect. K+ movement at rest and during depolarization is outward (efflux) down its concentration gradient, not inward -- and K+ efflux is associated with repolarization, not the ascending limb.
explanations.B: Correct. The ascending (rising) limb of the spike is depolarization itself -- the phase driven by rising Na+ permeability and Na+ influx that carries the membrane potential from rest, through threshold, to the overshoot. It is the mirror image of the descending limb, which represents repolarization instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Na+ influx that produces the ascending limb flows through voltage-gated Na+ channels, not leak channels -- leak channels are the resting-state pathway for K+, not the depolarizing pathway for Na+.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Repolarization is represented by the descending limb of the spike, not the ascending limb.
explanations.E: Incorrect as the single best answer here: while the initial part of depolarization is associated with rising excitability, option B names the ascending limb's actual identity (depolarization) directly, which is the more complete and specific description tested by this question.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the ascending limb of the spike as depolarization, driven by Na+ influx through voltage-gated channels.

questions.title: Threshold: Na+ channels triggered to open normally
questions.question: Threshold for production of an action potential in a nerve:

options.A: is a membrane potential (transmembrane voltage) at which the increase in K+ permeability exceeds the increase in Na+ permeability
options.B: is a condition where Na+ channels are triggered to open normally
options.C: is a condition where active Na+ transport stops
options.D: a & b are correct

explanations.A: Incorrect. This describes the opposite balance from the one that defines threshold: crossing threshold requires the rise in Na+ permeability to outpace the offsetting rise in K+ permeability, not the reverse.
explanations.B: Correct. Threshold is the membrane potential at which enough voltage-gated Na+ channels have opened, in the normal physiological way, that the resulting Na+ influx becomes self-sustaining (regenerative). Each opened channel's influx depolarizes the membrane further and opens still more channels, in a positive-feedback loop. This is what turns a fading, graded local response into a full, fixed-size, propagated action potential.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Na+-K+ pump (active Na+ transport) does not stop at threshold; it continues running throughout, restoring the ionic gradients the action potential runs down, a separate, slower process from the channel-gating event that defines threshold.
explanations.D: Incorrect, since option A is not correct -- only B correctly describes threshold.
explanations.E: Incorrect, since option B is correct.

questions.learning_objective: Define threshold as the membrane potential at which voltage-gated Na+ channel opening becomes regenerative.

questions.title: Excitability increased by hypocalcemia
questions.question: Excitability of the nerve is increased by:

options.A: hypercalcemia
options.B: hypokalemia
options.C: acidosis
options.D: hypocalcemia

explanations.A: Incorrect. A rise in extracellular calcium increases the membrane-stabilising effect on Na+ channels, raising the threshold and decreasing, not increasing, excitability.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A decrease in extracellular K+ (hypokalemia) hyperpolarizes the resting membrane, moving it further from threshold and decreasing excitability, not increasing it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acidosis is generally associated with decreased, not increased, nerve excitability -- the opposite direction from alkalosis, which increases it.
explanations.D: Correct. Extracellular calcium normally stabilises voltage-gated Na+ channels, raising the threshold needed to open them. A fall in extracellular calcium (hypocalcemia) removes some of that stabilisation, lowering the threshold and increasing excitability. This is the mechanism of hypocalcaemic tetany, in which spontaneous, repetitive firing produces sustained muscle contraction.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cooling generally slows and reduces nerve excitability and conduction rather than increasing it.

questions.learning_objective: State that hypocalcemia increases nerve excitability by reducing calcium's membrane-stabilising effect on Na+ channels.

questions.title: Absolute refractory period: excitability completely lost
questions.question: The absolute refractory period:

options.A: is a period during which excitability is completely lost
options.B: is a period during which stronger stimulus is needed to excite the muscle fiber
options.C: is coincided with the descending limb of the spike
options.D: is a period during which the excitability is less than normal

explanations.A: Correct. During the absolute refractory period, enough voltage-gated Na+ channels have their inactivation gates closed that no stimulus, however strong, can trigger a second action potential. Excitability is not merely reduced but completely lost until enough channels recover. This qualitative difference is exactly what separates the absolute from the relative refractory period.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Needing only a stronger-than-normal stimulus describes the relative refractory period, where some Na+ channels are still available; during the absolute refractory period, no stimulus strength suffices.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The absolute refractory period runs from roughly the start of depolarization through the early part of repolarization, not specifically coinciding with the descending limb (repolarization) alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Less than normal" describes the relative refractory period's reduced, but nonzero, excitability -- the absolute refractory period is qualitatively different, a complete, not partial, loss.
explanations.E: Incorrect, since option A correctly describes the absolute refractory period.

questions.learning_objective: State that the absolute refractory period is a period of completely lost excitability, distinct from the relative refractory period's merely reduced excitability.

questions.title: Absolute refractory period is associated with loss of excitability
questions.question: It is correct to say that:

options.A: subthreshold stimulus leads to an action potential
options.B: a decrease in Ca++ in ECF leads to a decrease in excitability in the nerve
options.C: a decrease in K+ in ECF leads to an increase in excitability in the nerve
options.D: absolute refractory period is associated with loss of excitability
options.E: absolute refractory period is associated with only a decrease in excitability

explanations.A: Incorrect. A subthreshold stimulus, by definition, is not strong enough to trigger the regenerative Na+ influx an action potential needs -- it produces only a fading local response, not a propagated action potential.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A decrease in extracellular Ca2+ removes some of calcium's membrane-stabilising effect on Na+ channels, lowering the threshold and increasing, not decreasing, excitability (hypocalcaemic tetany).
explanations.C: Incorrect. A decrease in extracellular K+ hyperpolarizes the resting membrane, moving it further from threshold, which decreases excitability rather than increasing it.
explanations.D: Correct. During the absolute refractory period, the Na+ channels needed to fire a second action potential have their inactivation gates closed and are unavailable, so the fibre's excitability is lost. No stimulus, however strong, can excite it until enough channels recover.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Describing the absolute refractory period as "only a decrease" understates it -- excitability during this period is not merely decreased but completely abolished, which is exactly what distinguishes it from the relative refractory period.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the absolute refractory period is associated with loss of excitability, distinguishing it from the calcium- and potassium-driven excitability changes in the other options.

questions.title: Nerve excitability increased by alkalosis
questions.question: Nerve excitability is increased by:

options.A: cooling
options.B: local anaesthetics
options.C: acidosis
options.D: deep pressure

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cooling generally slows nerve conduction and reduces excitability, not increases it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated Na+ channels, preventing the depolarizing permeability rise a nerve needs to fire, so they decrease, not increase, excitability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acidosis (a fall in blood pH) is associated with decreased nerve excitability, the opposite direction from alkalosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deep pressure on a nerve reduces or abolishes conduction, particularly in large A-type fibres, rather than increasing excitability.
explanations.E: Correct. Alkalosis (a rise in blood pH) lowers the amount of ionised (free) extracellular calcium, even without changing total calcium -- and it is the ionised fraction that exerts calcium's membrane-stabilising effect on Na+ channels. With less ionised calcium available to stabilise the channels, the threshold falls and excitability rises, which is why hyperventilation-induced alkalosis can produce the same tetany seen with true hypocalcemia.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that alkalosis increases nerve excitability by lowering ionised extracellular calcium, the same mechanism family as hypocalcaemic tetany.

questions.title: Excitability is zero during the absolute refractory period
questions.question: The excitability of the nerve is zero during:

options.A: super normal phase of excitability
options.B: relative refractory period
options.C: sub normal phase of excitability
options.D: local response

explanations.A: Incorrect. The supernormal phase, which follows the refractory periods, is a window of increased (not zero) excitability, when a smaller-than-normal stimulus can excite the fibre.
explanations.B: Incorrect. During the relative refractory period excitability is reduced but not zero -- a stronger-than-threshold stimulus can still trigger a second action potential.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The subnormal phase is a period of reduced, not zero, excitability that can follow the supernormal phase, related to lingering after-hyperpolarization.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The local response is itself accompanied by increased excitability (it moves the membrane closer to the firing level), the opposite of zero excitability.
explanations.E: Correct. During the absolute refractory period, enough voltage-gated Na+ channels have their inactivation gates closed that no stimulus, however strong, can excite the fibre. Excitability is genuinely zero, not merely reduced, which is what distinguishes it from every other phase of the excitability cycle.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the absolute refractory period as the only phase of the excitability cycle during which excitability is genuinely zero.

questions.title: Negative energy balance causes loss of body weight
questions.question: About the energy balance:

options.A: In normal adults, the energy intake is greater than the energy output.
options.B: During growth, the energy intake is equal to the energy output.
options.C: With a negative energy balance, there is loss of the body weight.
options.D: In obesity, there is increased protein content of the body.

explanations.A: Incorrect. In a normal, weight-stable adult, energy intake equals energy output -- a stable weight is exactly the sign that the two are matched, not that intake exceeds output.
explanations.B: Incorrect. During growth, intake must exceed output, since part of the surplus energy is laid down as new tissue rather than expended; equal intake and output would leave no energy for growth.
explanations.C: Correct. When energy output exceeds energy intake (a negative energy balance), the body must draw on its own stores, chiefly fat, to make up the deficit. The result is loss of body weight, which is the direct, expected consequence of a sustained energy deficit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Obesity reflects a sustained positive energy balance and is characterised by increased fat content in the body, not increased protein content.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that a negative energy balance (output exceeding intake) causes loss of body weight.

questions.title: Most catabolic energy appears as heat
questions.question: Most of the energy released from catabolic processes:

options.A: Appears as thermal (heat) energy.
options.B: Is stored as high energy phosphate bonds.
options.C: Is used by the kidneys to perform osmotic work.
options.D: is used for building new protoplasm.

explanations.A: Correct. Most of the chemical energy released when a foodstuff is catabolised is dissipated as heat rather than captured as usable work. The body's metabolic machinery is far from perfectly efficient, and even the fraction captured in ATP is itself released as heat once that ATP is spent on cellular work.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Only a minority of catabolic energy is captured as high-energy phosphate bonds (ATP); the majority is lost as heat, not stored this way.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal osmotic work consumes only a small fraction of total metabolic energy, far short of "most" of the energy released from catabolism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Building new protoplasm (anabolism, growth) accounts for only a small fraction of total energy expenditure in an adult at energy balance, not the majority of catabolic energy release.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that most of the energy released from catabolic processes appears as heat.

questions.title: Carbohydrate physical heat value equals physiological heat value
questions.question: The physical heat value of:

options.A: Food is measured by the respirometer.
options.B: Carbohydrate is equal to its physiological heat value.
options.C: Protein is 9.3 Kcal /gm.
options.D: Fat is 5.3 Kcal/gm

explanations.A: Incorrect. Physical heat value is measured by burning a weighed sample in a bomb calorimeter, not a respirometer -- a respirometer instead measures O2 consumption and CO2 production for indirect calorimetry.
explanations.B: Correct. Carbohydrate is fully oxidised by the body just as it is in a bomb calorimeter, so its physical heat value and its physiological heat value are the same, about 4.1 Kcal/g. This is unlike protein, whose nitrogen-containing portion the body cannot fully oxidise, so its physiological value is lower than its physical value.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 9.3 Kcal/g is the physical heat value of fat, not protein; protein's physical heat value is about 5.3 Kcal/g.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 5.3 Kcal/g is the physical heat value of protein, not fat; fat's physical heat value is about 9.3 Kcal/g -- this option and option C swap the two figures.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that carbohydrate's physical and physiological heat values are equal, and identify the correct physical heat values for protein and fat.

questions.title: Metabolism of 10 g protein produces about 41 Kcal
questions.question: The metabolism of 10 gm protein inside the body would produce:

options.A: 53 Kcal.
options.B: 93 Kcal.
options.C: 410 Kcal.
options.D: 41 Kcal.

explanations.A: Incorrect. 53 Kcal would follow from protein's physical (bomb calorimeter) heat value of 5.3 Kcal/g, not the physiological value the body actually derives from protein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 93 Kcal has no straightforward basis in either protein's physical or physiological heat value for a 10 g sample; it does not correspond to a standard teaching figure here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 410 Kcal would follow only from a tenfold arithmetic error (41 Kcal/g instead of 4.1 Kcal/g); no standard heat value for protein approaches 41 Kcal/g.
explanations.D: Correct. The body cannot fully oxidise protein's nitrogen-containing portion, excreting it as urea instead, so protein's physiological heat value (about 4.1 Kcal/g) is lower than its physical value (about 5.3 Kcal/g). For 10 g of protein, that physiological value gives about 41 Kcal. This is the energy actually available to the body, not the larger figure a bomb calorimeter would report.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Calculate that metabolising 10 g of protein yields about 41 Kcal, using protein's physiological (not physical) heat value.

questions.title: RQ above one, EXCEPT: gluconeogenesis from fat lowers RQ
questions.question: A respiratory quotient above one occurs in all the following cases except:

options.A: Hyperventilation.
options.B: Muscular exercise.
options.C: Fevers and acidosis.
options.D: Transformation of carbohydrate into fat.
options.E: Gluconcogenesis using fat as a substrate to be converted into glucose.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Hyperventilation blows off CO2 faster than the underlying metabolic rate would otherwise produce it, which can transiently push the measured (apparent) RQ above 1.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Heavy muscular exercise generates extra CO2 from bicarbonate buffering of lactic acid, on top of the CO2 from substrate oxidation, which can raise the measured RQ above 1.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Fever and acidosis both drive compensatory hyperventilation and altered metabolism that can raise CO2 output relative to O2 uptake, pushing RQ above 1.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Converting carbohydrate into fat (lipogenesis) releases more CO2 than the O2 it consumes, which is the classic cause of a sustained RQ above 1, sometimes well above it.
explanations.E: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). Gluconeogenesis that uses fat as the substrate to build new glucose runs in the opposite metabolic direction from lipogenesis. It requires relatively more O2 uptake for the CO2 it produces, which lowers the RQ rather than raising it above 1. This is exactly why it is the exception among these otherwise RQ-raising conditions.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify that gluconeogenesis using fat as the substrate for glucose lowers, rather than raises, the respiratory quotient.

questions.title: Respiratory quotient is about 1 in the brain
questions.question: The respiratory quotient (RO):

options.A: Is the ratio of the volume of O2 consumed to that of CO₂ produced.
options.B: Rises in the second week of starvation.
options.C: Is 0.7 when glucose is the metabolized substrate.
options.D: Is about 1 in the brain.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This inverts the definition -- the respiratory quotient is the ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed, not O2 consumed to CO2 produced.
explanations.B: Incorrect. RQ falls, not rises, as starvation progresses into its second week, since the body shifts increasingly toward fat oxidation (and later ketone bodies) as glucose stores run out, and fat's RQ (~0.7) is lower than carbohydrate's.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.7 is the RQ for fat oxidation, not glucose; glucose (carbohydrate) oxidation gives an RQ close to 1.0, since carbohydrate already contains enough oxygen within its own molecule to need relatively less added O2.
explanations.D: Correct. The brain normally metabolises almost exclusively glucose, so the RQ of brain tissue runs close to 1, matching carbohydrate's characteristic value. This makes the brain a useful example of how RQ tracks the fuel actually being oxidised.
explanations.E: Incorrect. An uncontrolled diabetic cannot use glucose effectively and relies instead on fat oxidation (with ketone body formation), giving a low RQ, not one near 1.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the respiratory quotient is about 1 in the brain, which metabolises almost exclusively glucose.

questions.title: Excess R.O. indicates the fuel used during exercise
questions.question: The excess R.O.:

options.A: is the R.Q. determined during sleep.
options.B: Indicates the fuel used during a certain exercise.
options.C: Determination requires estimation of the O2, consumption and CO, production during the recovery period only.
options.D: Is about 1 in a prolonged exercise and 0.7 in short exercises.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The excess R.O. is measured in relation to exercise and its recovery, not during sleep -- sleep is an unrelated resting state with its own separate metabolic rate.
explanations.B: Correct. The respiratory exchange ratio measured around a bout of exercise reflects which fuel is being drawn on. A ratio closer to 1 points to carbohydrate as the dominant fuel, while a ratio closer to 0.7 points to fat. Tracking it therefore indicates the fuel used during that particular exercise.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Characterising the fuel used during exercise draws on gas exchange measured during the exercise itself, not on the recovery period alone -- restricting the estimate to recovery-only measurements would miss the exercise-period substrate use this option itself asks about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This reverses the expected pattern: prolonged, lower-intensity exercise tends to draw more on fat oxidation (a ratio nearer 0.7), while short, intense exercise draws more on carbohydrate and anaerobic glycolysis (a ratio nearer or above 1), not the other way around.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the respiratory ratio measured around exercise indicates which fuel is being used during that exercise.

field_notes.authorDoubt: The bank prints "excess R.O." without expanding the abbreviation; read here as the respiratory exchange ratio associated with an exercise bout and its oxygen-debt recovery, consistent with option A's own comparison to R.Q. Flagged in the concept's own uncertainty field.

questions.title: BMR, EXCEPT: not measured immediately after dinner
questions.question: About the BMR, all the following is true except:

options.A: It is expressed in Kcal /square meter/hour.
options.B: Normally, it is about 40 Kcal in young adult males.
options.C: It represents the energy expenditure needed for activity of the vital organs
options.D: It is slightly higher in males and is maximal in children at the age of 5 years
options.E: It is measured immediately after dinner at an atmospheric temp about 10 C.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. BMR is conventionally expressed per unit body surface area per hour (Kcal/m²/hour), which allows comparison between people of different sizes.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. About 40 Kcal/m²/hour is the standard teaching figure for BMR in a young adult male.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. BMR represents the minimum energy expenditure needed to keep the vital organs (heart, brain, kidneys, and the rest) running at complete rest.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. BMR is slightly higher in males than females, and is at its highest in early childhood, around age 5, gradually declining thereafter.
explanations.E: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). A valid BMR measurement requires an overnight fast, not immediately after a meal, since eating raises metabolic rate through specific dynamic action. It also requires a thermoneutral room temperature, not a cold environment such as 10C, which would itself drive up heat production through cold-induced thermogenesis. Measuring right after dinner in a cold room would inflate the reading well above the true basal value.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.subtopic: Basal metabolic rate and specific dynamic action
questions.learning_objective: Identify that BMR must be measured fasting and at thermoneutral temperature, not immediately after a meal in a cold room.

questions.title: Energy equivalent of oxygen: heat produced per litre O2 consumed
questions.question: The energy equivalent of oxygen is

options.A: The amount of heat (Kcal) produced when one litre of O2 is consumed.
options.B: Used for estimation of the metabolic rate by direct calorimetry.
options.C: About 5 Kcal /L in case of fats and 4.7 Kcal /L in case of carbohydrates.
options.D: About 4.8 Kcal /L in case of proteins and 4.6 Kcal /L in the post-absorptive
options.E: Not equal to the heat value of O₂.

explanations.A: Correct. The energy equivalent of oxygen is defined as the amount of heat, in Kcal, produced when one litre of O2 is consumed in oxidising a given substrate. It is the same heat-value idea as a foodstuff's caloric value, restated from the oxygen-consumption side. Its exact figure varies with which substrate is being oxidised.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The energy equivalent of oxygen is the basis of indirect calorimetry (estimating metabolic rate from measured O2 consumption), not direct calorimetry, which instead measures heat output directly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This reverses the standard figures: carbohydrate's energy equivalent of O2 (about 5 Kcal/L) is higher than fat's (about 4.7 Kcal/L), not the other way around, since carbohydrate needs relatively less O2 to produce a given amount of CO2 and heat.
explanations.D: Incorrect. These specific protein and post-absorptive figures do not represent the standard definitional fact the question tests; the energy equivalent of oxygen is defined generally (option A), and its exact value depends on which substrate is being oxidised rather than a single fixed protein-specific figure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The energy equivalent of oxygen essentially is a restatement of a substrate's heat value expressed per litre of O2 consumed, not a separate, unequal quantity.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define the energy equivalent of oxygen as the heat produced when one litre of O2 is consumed.

questions.title: SDA, EXCEPT: not due to the work of digestion and absorption
questions.question: About the specific dynamic action (SDA), all the following is true except:

options.A: It is an increase in the metabolic rate after food intake.
options.B: The SDA of proteins is about 30% and is due mainly to its metabolism in the liver
options.C: It is generally due to the work done during digestion and absorption of food.
options.D: Normally, it is about 6 % for carbohydrates and 4 % for fats.
options.E: It is used for warming the body on exposure to a cold weather.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Specific dynamic action is, by definition, the rise in metabolic rate that follows eating.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Protein produces the largest SDA of the three foodstuffs, about 30%, driven mainly by the metabolic cost of processing absorbed amino acids (chiefly deamination) in the liver.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). SDA is caused mainly by the metabolic processing of the absorbed nutrients afterward, not by the mechanical work of digesting and absorbing the food itself. This is exactly why protein, whose metabolic processing (deamination) is energetically costly, produces by far the largest SDA. Digestion and absorption work itself is not dramatically different across foodstuffs, so it cannot explain protein's outsized effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Carbohydrate's SDA is about 6% and fat's is about 4%, both well below protein's 30%.
explanations.E: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. The extra heat SDA generates can contribute to warming the body on exposure to cold, alongside other thermogenic mechanisms.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.subtopic: Basal metabolic rate and specific dynamic action
questions.learning_objective: Identify that specific dynamic action is caused mainly by the metabolic processing of absorbed nutrients, not by the mechanical work of digestion and absorption.
